courses.actualFullProfile: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
courses.shortDescription: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courses.contribution: Year1PPD:personal/academicdevelopment,not disciplinaryequivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
courses.shortDescription: This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
courses.contribution: teaches accounting theory and practice and how to read and analyse financial statements and corporate annual reports; it offers related content for Accounting and Financial Reporting Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: As we enter the “Age of AI,” this course explores AI’s business, managerial, economic, and societal implications. It is designed for UCR students with a strong interest in AI and requires no prior technical background. The course traces AI’s evolution from early research to generative AI, highlighting its capabilities and limits. Through real-world examples and business cases, students analyse AI’s impact on competitiveness, innovation, labour markets, economic growth, inequality, climate change and society. In this context, students critically examine AI governance and ethics, addressing issues such as bias, privacy, and fairness across business functions (e.g. Marketing, HR, Finance), while also exploring corporate governance and regulation more broadly.
courses.shortDescription: This course examines how organizations are structured and evolve over time. It explores how organizational design relates to strategy, external environment, human behavior, culture, governance and performance. A particular emphasis is put on discussing the concept and enabling capabilities of organizational agility required to navigate a fast-paced world and tackle increased uncertainty.
courses.contribution: Actual fullprofile studiesAIeffects oncompetitiveness,innovation,labourmarkets,growth,inequality andcorporategovernance/privacy/bias. Directbusiness/economictechnology content; not anorganisation-design course,complete labour economics or formal informationvaluation. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course introduces students to the legal frameworks governing business transactions in a globalized economy. It examines how law shapes cross-border trade, contracts, sales of goods and services, intellectual property, foreign investment, and digital commerce. Emphasis is placed on the practical application of legal rules to real-world business scenarios, as well as on comparative and international perspectives. Through interactive class discussions, problem - based assignments, quizzes, and an arbitration simulation, students develop the analytical and practical skills needed to identify legal risks and design effective solutions in transnational business contexts.
courses.shortDescription: Businesses and entrepreneurs are confronted with legal complexity not only at the domestic level but particularly across divergent legal systems. This course presents a survey of the most essential fields of business law: contracts law, company law, trade law, intellectual property, and dispute resolution. An ultimate aim of the course is to critically examine the impact of globalization and digitization on the development of business law.
courses.contribution: Legalframeworks forcross-bordertransactions,contracts,investment,intellectualproperty anddigitalcommerce withcases/arbitration. Directbusinesslaw;not institutional-economics transaction-costmodels or specialistITlaw. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course develops practical financial decision-making skills through case studies and real-world applications. Students learn to analyze financial data, assess risks, and make informed investment, budgeting, and business decisions that enhance value, financial security, and long-term planning.
courses.shortDescription: This course develops practical financial decision-making skills through case studies and real-world applications. Students learn to analyze financial data, assess risks, and make informed investment, budgeting, and business decisions that enhance value, financial security, and long-term planning.
courses.contribution: develops financial decision-making through case studies: analysing financial data, assessing risk and making investment, budgeting and business decisions; it offers related content for Finance Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.
courses.shortDescription: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
courses.contribution: teaches the principles of microeconomics (supply and demand, game theory, consumer behaviour, the theory of the firm, market structure) and macroeconomics (aggregate output, unemployment, inflation, short-run goods and financial markets); it offers related content for the first-year Microeconomics and Macroeconomics foundation Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course explores the economy as a whole by examining its dynamics over the short, medium, and long run. Key indicators such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment are studied. The course analyses how fiscal and monetary polici es affect the economy. It also covers business cycles, economic crises, and international trade, providing the tools needed to interpret economic data, evaluate policy decisions, and understand global economic trends.
courses.shortDescription: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
courses.contribution: analyses national income, growth, inflation and unemployment, fiscal and monetary policy, business cycles, economic crises and international trade; it offers related content for Macroeconomics and the macroeconomic-policy, crisis and trade content of the Economics specialisation Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of advanced topics in microeconomic theory. Structured in three parts, the course begins with an in-depth analysis of consumer behaviour, including decision-making under uncertainty, non -egoistic preferences, and cognitive limitations. The second part analyses market structures with an emphasis on imperfect competition, strategic behaviour, and the functioning of factor markets. The final part of the course covers general equilibrium and market efficiency, investigating externalities and the role of government in the economy. Throughout the course, students will engage with research papers through presentations and discussions, bridging theoretical concepts with empirical evidence.
courses.shortDescription: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
courses.contribution: teaches advanced microeconomic theory: decision-making under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, imperfect competition and strategic behaviour, general equilibrium, market efficiency and externalities, with research papers; it offers related content for Microeconomics: Choices, Markets and Welfare and the consumer-behaviour questions of the Economics specialisation Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course examines the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy affects efficiency and equity. It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.
courses.shortDescription: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
courses.contribution: examines the role of government in the economy: market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, public spending, redistribution and political economy; it offers related content for Public Economics and the role of the state in the economy Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
courses.shortDescription: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
courses.contribution: OLS,GLS,IV estimators,t/F/LM tests,samplingdistributions,MonteCarlo/Stata andanempiricalpaper. Directeconometricmethods for economicrelationships; important regressionpart ofQMIII,not its optimisation/integration/dynamic-systems half or anindividualthesis. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
courses.shortDescription: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
courses.contribution: integrates psychology into economic theory through biases, heuristics, framing and experiments on decision-making; it offers related content for the psychological perspective that the Economics specialisation combines with economics Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Grounded in academic theory, real-world applications, and case studies, this course unpacks what drives consumers’ behaviour and engagement with brands, and how marketers can build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key concepts related to marketing strategy and consumer psychology and examines external forces influencing reinvention of the Marketing function, including digital and AI-driven marketing. Drawing on the work of Kotler, Aaker, Kapferer and other leading scholars, students will explore real-life case studies, develop marketing plans and learn how to create effective brand strategies for greater consumer engagement.
courses.shortDescription: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation, and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build sustainable brand strategies.
courses.contribution: covers marketing strategy, consumer psychology and consumer engagement, with marketing plans and brand strategy; it offers related content for the marketing half of Management of Organisations and Marketing Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
courses.shortDescription: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
courses.contribution: has students develop a strategic plan from vision to execution and examine strategy and business models under technological change; it offers related content for the strategy part of management and organisational strategy Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas—perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.
courses.shortDescription: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas—perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.
courses.contribution: Planning andconductingmarketresearch,collecting/analyzingdata andreporting forbusiness decisions. Specificbusiness-researchtraining,not the8ECindividualresearchthesis. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
courses.shortDescription: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
courses.contribution: Institutional,political andculturalforces shapingglobalbusiness,cross-bordergovernance,corporateresponsibility,geopoliticalstrategy andtrade. Directinternationalbusiness subject;contextual toEconomicsandGlobalChallenges,not its introductory economic-model toolkit. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: In this course, you will develop a new venture idea from the ground up. No prior business experience is required – working in teams you will learn by doing, developing a startup concept from ideation through to the final pitch. Along the way, you will gain essential business and entrepreneurial skills, including design thinking, market validation and business planning. This course fosters creativity, business acumen and collaboration to drive business and social entrepreneurship.
courses.shortDescription: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
courses.contribution: has teams develop a venture from ideation to pitch through market validation and business planning; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the business and management foundations of Management of Organisations and Marketing and is the formal prerequisite for Money, Banking & Finance, Strategy & Digital Transformation, International Business & Governance and Market Research Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
courses.shortDescription: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
courses.contribution: covers research design, sampling and descriptive and inferential statistics including analysis of variance; it offers related content for the statistical part of the programme's quantitative methods training and is the formal prerequisite for the economics and business courses that follow Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Leadership & Diversity Management explores how diverse perspectives and experiences shape effective leadership in dynamic, varied environments. Blending cutting-edge theories with hands-on practice, students develop the skills to lead with empathy, inclusivity, and adaptability. Through engaging case studies, interactive workshops, and reflective assessments, participants build awareness of diversity and learn to inspire ethical, collaborative teams.
courses.shortDescription: Leadership & Diversity Management explores how diverse perspectives and experiences shape effective leadership in dynamic, varied environments. Blending cutting-edge theories with hands-on practice, students develop the skills to lead with empathy, inclusivity, and adaptability. Through engaging case studies, interactive workshops, and reflective assessments, participants build awareness of diversity and learn to inspire ethical, collaborative teams.
courses.contribution: explores how diverse perspectives and experiences shape effective, inclusive leadership, with case studies and workshops; it makes a specific complementary contribution to working across cultures in diverse business environments Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: People are the organisation. Without people, organisations cannot survive or be productive. This course, tailored for Liberal Arts and Sciences bachelor students, offers an interdisciplinary exploration of the psychological, social, and structural dynamics within organisations. It equips students with the knowledge and skills needed to navigate and influence organisational environments effectively throughout their academic and professional careers. Drawing on foundational and contemporary research in organisational behaviour, this upper- level undergraduate course incorporates a case-based approach that includes conceptual frameworks, case discussions, and skill-building activities. Students will explore topics such as motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and organizational culture using Robbins and Judge’s (2023) Organisational Behaviour as a primary resource. Additional literature and materials will supplement the course to provide a well-rounded perspective. Topics Covered => Core Concepts: Diversity in organisations, attitudes and job satisfaction, emotions and moods, personality and values, perception and decision-making, motivation, communication, leadership, power and politics, and conflict and negotiation. Structural Dynamics: The structure and culture of organisations, group behaviour, work teams, and organisational change. These topics are structured within a comprehensive model that defines the field of organisational behaviour and outlines its key concepts and relationships.
courses.shortDescription: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
courses.contribution: covers organisational behaviour, motivation, leadership, group dynamics, organisational culture and decision-making through cases; it offers related content for the organisations part of Management of Organisations and Marketing Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Developments in AI are transforming the nature of human interaction and raising fundamental questions concerning human flourishing and its alignment with technological progress. This course examines these issues from both philosophical and psychological pe rspectives, while exploring the deep connections between the two fields. In a module on the ethics of AI, we'll consider ramifications of the use of AI in the context of moral inquiry. Core topics include AI fairness and bias , privacy, responsibility and accountability . We will also approach the question concerning the moral status of AI systems , and some of the broader implications of AI, focusing on existential risks and broad political implications of the use of AI. In a module on psychology of AI, we will examine what it means to be human when AI systems increasingly mirror or simulate uniquely human capabilities. Research shows that people may both over-trust and resist AI in decision-making, which subsequently raises questions on responsibility and agency. In clinical and therapeutic contexts, AI challenges ideas of empathy, confidentiality, and the therapeutic alliance, while in organisational and social domains, algorithmic biases reflect and amplify existing stereotypes. Developmentally, AI companions and tutors shape how children learn and relate, prompting concerns about attachment and socialisation.
courses.shortDescription: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
courses.contribution: examines AI fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility and accountability from philosophical and psychological perspectives; it offers related content for the ethical questions of information technology Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
courses.shortDescription: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.

Realcomputationaldecisionmethod; not economicvaluationofinformation or aninformation-economics course. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
courses.shortDescription: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
courses.contribution: introduces relational database theory, SQL, normalisation and query processing; it makes a specific complementary contribution to organising information so that it has value for businesses Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Software development is designing, creating, testing, and maintaining software applications. We learn to program in C++, which offers fine-grained control over system resources, and in Haskell, which is a purely functional programming language. Various stages of software development such as planning and requirements gathering, testing and quality assurance, deployment and maintenance is covered in laboratory format consisting mostly on in-class discussions and code reviews. Projects are undertaken to provide experience of programming in C++ and in Haskell. There are written Midterm and Final exams.
courses.shortDescription: Covers software design, creation, testing and maintenance. Uses C++ and Haskell and covers planning, requirements gathering, testing, deployment and maintenance through discussions and code reviews.
courses.contribution: Softwareengineeringstages,requirements,testing andmaintenance throughC++/Haskellprojects. Technicalsoftwareconstruction,not a fullbusinessinformation-systemdesign orknowledgemanagementcourse. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course aims to provide the student with knowledge, skills and critical thinking ability in algorithm design and analysis. Inappropriate choice of algorithm and associated data structure can seriously impact on the performance of an application. The st udy of algorithm design and analysis provides techniques which help minimize the execution time of an algorithm. An emphasis is on the experimental performance analysis of algorithms. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Larger algorithm projects are also undertaken. There is a written midterm exam and a written final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained an understanding of how algorithms have helped shape the modern world.
courses.shortDescription: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
courses.contribution: teaches algorithm design and analysis and data structures with experimental performance analysis; it makes a specific complementary contribution to how information is efficiently organised and processed in information systems Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
courses.shortDescription: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
courses.contribution: Actual data cleaning,manipulation,visualisation andspatial/textdata with a researchproject. Generaldata-method training; neither anindividual economicsthesis nor dedicated economic-research domain is guaranteed. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.
courses.shortDescription: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
courses.contribution: teaches linear regression, classification, resampling, tree-based methods and clustering with real-world applications; it makes a specific complementary contribution to using data to predict the economic consequences of technologies Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This is the gateway course of Computer Science and AI studies; an introductory course in problem solving and computer programming in Python. The course begins by introducing traditional structured programming and data constructs (i.e. branching, loops, functions; tuples and lists). Then consideration is given to testing and debugging and finally the object- oriented programming constructs. During the entire semester, elements of discrete mathematics (e.g., logic, sets, enumeration) as well as certain computational problem solving techniques are also incorporated into the course material. There are classes twice a week. The first half of each class is a lecture where we learn new material, while the second half is devoted to laboratory work where students tackle programming exercises and demonstrate their work. Homework comprises weekly programming exercises and online quizzes. Two larger programming projects are undertaken. There is a written Midterm exam and a written Final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with the Python programming language as well as important concepts of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving techniques.
courses.shortDescription: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
courses.contribution: teaches Python programming, structured and object-oriented problem solving, testing and debugging; it makes a specific complementary contribution to applying information technology to business and is the formal prerequisite for Decision-making in AI, Software Development and Algorithms & Data Structures Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3
courses.shortDescription: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
courses.contribution: teaches differentiation, integration and differential equations with projects that include economics; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the mathematical toolkit of the quantitative methods sequence and is the formal prerequisite for Probability & Statistics Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
courses.shortDescription: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
courses.contribution: covers probability theory, distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; it directly supplies the probability and statistical inference that econometrics and quantitative economic analysis rely on Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions. The first part of this course introduces you to the basic conceptual tools for understanding governance and to the major fault line in tackling sustainability problems as identified by Charles Mann in “The Wizard and the Prophet”. Wizards are techno-optimists who believe humanity’s creativity can tackle every challenge, whilst Prophets argue that humans should take a holistic and systemic approach that calls for a drastic reduction of exploiting the earth resources to respect planetary boundaries. In the second part of the course, we use Problem Based Learning to examine governance solutions to concrete sustainability challenges regarding food, freshwater, energy, and climate change.
courses.shortDescription: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
courses.contribution: examines how sustainability policy is made and enforced at local, national and international levels, which actors are influential and what makes policy effective; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the sustainable-development and policy questions of the Emerging Markets specialisation Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.
courses.shortDescription: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
courses.contribution: introduces the legal, social and normative perspectives on law, legal systems, property law and contract law; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the legal and social questions of the information society, but it offers no information-technology law Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: This course is about great powers, superpowers and even hyperpowers. ‘Empire’ is a powerful and dangerous word. It has a rich and ambiguous history and strong polemical connotations now and in the past. The typical empire is usually presented as oppressive and ruthless, although some of the modern empires are democracies that focus upon the improvements of its society. This course deals with some of the most important empires in World History. Next to this some of the most important theories on empires will be treated. How is the rise and fall of empires explained? What are the sources of empire and how are great power politics conducted?
courses.shortDescription: Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.
courses.contribution: treats great powers, empires, the theories of their rise and fall and power politics; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the historical and power-political background of rising economic powers, and does not cover their economies Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
courses.shortDescription: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
courses.contribution: teaches theories of moral reasoning and practical ethics, including equality and climate change; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the responsible management and policy decisions strand of the Emerging Markets specialisation Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.
courses.shortDescription: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
courses.contribution: teaches how to analyse and compare political systems and institutions and the impact of globalisation; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the institutions and role of the state that Economic Growth and Institutions and Institutional Economics address Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Brewing wars in the South China Sea, the Middle East, and Europe, trade wars, global climate change, amongst a plethora of other crises and difficulties, show the importance of understanding International Relations and geopolitics. This course gives the student a basic understanding of International Relations through a historical and contemporary scope. You work with a textbook to understand the different schools of thought within International Relations and then use historical or contemporary topics to apply these theories to. This will be achieved by group presentations. Your knowledge will be further increased by homework assignments and an exam. Finally, you end the course with a United Nations Security Council Simulation, where you take on the role of one of the UNSC members, and plead your country’s case in a current problem of international relations.
courses.shortDescription: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
courses.contribution: Internationalrelationstheories,historical/currentgeopolitics andUNsimulation. Context forinternationalbusiness andpoliticaleconomy;not formal international-trade economics. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
courses.shortDescription: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
courses.contribution: introduces the concepts, methods and theories of sociology and the links between local societies and global phenomena; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the sociological perspective that the Economics specialisation combines with economics Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
courses.shortDescription: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courses.contribution: Qualitativeresearchdesign,collection,analysis,interpretation andreflexivity throughteamprojects. Contextualinquiry into political/cultural processes;not quantitative economics or anindividual economics thesis. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
courses.shortDescription: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
courses.contribution: examines the development of sociology in the context of imperialism and colonial responses and the debates about modernity; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the historical and cultural background of developing economies, not to their economics Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.
courses.shortDescription: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
courses.contribution: examines civil society, solidarity, social capital and social trust from a global perspective in contemporary social theory; it makes a specific complementary contribution to how culture and social institutions shape the business environment Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.

courses.actualFullProfile: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.
courses.shortDescription: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
courses.contribution: Actual multivariate statistics: linear/logistic regression,factoranalysis,ANOVA/ANCOVA andnonparametric tests withanalyses/reporting. Complementaryquantitativepreparation; no guaranteed experimental-design course or individual thesis. Whole course:7.5EC; contextual contributions do not become specialist equivalence.
